title: MATH 107: Introduction to Linear Algebra
text:
Welcome
This website contains materials for MATH 107: Introduction to Linear Algebra (3 units, GE Area 2) at Cal Poly Humboldt. Class meets face to face Monday, Wednesday, and Friday, 10:00–10:50 a.m., in FR 201.
Catalog description: Euclidean spaces, matrices and matrix arithmetic, solving systems of equations, and eigenvalues and eigenvectors. Emphasis on applications and use of computation.
This site follows three units: representing and comparing things with vectors; transforming, solving, simulating, and computing with matrices; then explaining dynamics, fitting data, and exploiting structure (eigenvectors, least squares, SVD). Daily learning objectives are on Lectures. Class outlines for later meetings will be posted before those days.

title: MATH 107: Introduction to Linear Algebra
text:
What you’ll learn
By the end of the course you should be able to:

Interpret matrices, vectors, and complex numbers, both algebraically and geometrically.
Solve systems of linear equations using row-reduction techniques by hand and with software.
Find eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a matrix by hand for a \(2\times 2\) matrix and with software for general cases.
Understand and apply eigenvalues and eigenvectors to solve problems.
Recognize special types of matrices and their properties, such as triangular, symmetric, and positive definite matrices.
Communicate in the language of linear algebra, including linear combination, subspace, span, independence, basis, and dimension.
Write or adapt programs to implement linear algebra concepts, such as matrix arithmetic, vectors, and plotting.
Apply linear algebra to real-world problems.
Learn independently as well as collaboratively. Develop study techniques that include pre- and post-reading of class materials and be able to critically analyze and implement solutions in a team setting.

Daily objectives for each meeting are on the lectures page.

title: Lecture 07 — Norm, distance, RMS, and variation
text:
Learning objectives
By the end of class, students should be able to:

Compute vector norms and distances.
Interpret norm and distance geometrically and contextually.
Relate norm to RMS and, where appropriate, variation around an average.
Use software to calculate distances in dimensions too large for hand computation.

title: Lecture 07 — Norm, distance, RMS, and variation
text:
Warm-up
Let \(u=(3,-4)\) and \(v=(0,5)\).

Compute \(u^{\mathsf{T}}u\) and \(\sqrt{u^{\mathsf{T}}u}\) by hand.
Without a calculator, which is larger: \(\lVert u\rVert\) or \(\lVert v\rVert\)? Brief reason.

title: Lecture 07 — Norm, distance, RMS, and variation
text:
Fill in
The Euclidean norm of an \(n\)-vector \(x\) is \[
\lVert x\rVert = \sqrt{x_1^2+\cdots+x_n^2} = \sqrt{\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}}.
\] It measures the \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) of \(x\). For a scalar, \(\lVert x\rVert\) is the \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\).
Key properties (same size vectors; \(\beta\) a scalar): - \(\lVert \beta x\rVert = \underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\,\lVert x\rVert\) - \(\lVert x+y\rVert \leq \lVert x\rVert + \lVert y\rVert\) (triangle inequality) - \(\lVert x\rVert \geq 0\), and \(\lVert x\rVert=0\) only when \(x=\underline{\hspace{1.2cm}}\)
The RMS (root-mean-square) value is \[
\mathrm{rms}(x) = \frac{\lVert x\rVert}{\sqrt{n}} = \sqrt{\frac{x_1^2+\cdots+x_n^2}{n}}.
\] It describes a \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\) size of an entry, and is useful when comparing vectors of different \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\).
The distance between \(n\)-vectors \(a\) and \(b\) is \[
\mathrm{dist}(a,b) = \lVert a-b\rVert.
\] Geometrically this is the length of the \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\) from \(a\) to \(b\). Two vectors are “close” when this distance is \(\underline{\hspace{1.6cm}}\) (relative to the application).
The average is \(\mathrm{avg}(x)=\frac{1}{n}\mathbf{1}^{\mathsf{T}}x\). The de-meaned vector is \(\tilde{x}=x-\mathrm{avg}(x)\mathbf{1}\). The standard deviation is \[
\mathrm{std}(x)=\mathrm{rms}(\tilde{x})=\frac{\lVert x-\mathrm{avg}(x)\mathbf{1}\rVert}{\sqrt{n}},
\] which measures typical \(\underline{\hspace{2.8cm}}\) of the entries from their average.
Boyd’s identity: \(\mathrm{rms}(x)^2 = \mathrm{avg}(x)^2 + \mathrm{std}(x)^2\).

title: Lecture 07 — Norm, distance, RMS, and variation
text:
Software (keep this page open)
In this course we use either Octave or Python for norms and distances.
Octave (column vectors are fine):
x = [3; -4; 0];
norm(x)                 % Euclidean norm
sqrt(x'*x)              % same idea via the inner product
y = [1; 2; -1];
norm(x-y)               % distance ||x-y||
Python (NumPy):
import numpy as np
x = np.array([3.0, -4.0, 0.0])
np.linalg.norm(x)       # Euclidean norm
np.sqrt(x @ x)          # same idea via the inner product
y = np.array([1.0, 2.0, -1.0])
np.linalg.norm(x - y)   # distance ||x-y||
Handy formulas (either language): - \(\mathrm{rms}(x)=\lVert x\rVert/\sqrt{n}\) - \(\mathrm{avg}(x)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_i x_i\) (Octave mean(x), Python np.mean(x)) - \(\mathrm{std}(x)\) in Boyd’s sense is the RMS of the de-meaned vector (population form with divisor \(n\), not \(n-1\))

title: Lecture 07 — Norm, distance, RMS, and variation
text:
Worked in class
W1. Norm by hand and by software (Lachniet-style). Let \[
u = (2,\ -4,\ 0).
\] (a) Compute \(\lVert u\rVert\) by hand using \(\sqrt{u^{\mathsf{T}}u}\).

Write the Octave command and the Python command that compute the same value. What should both print?
Form the unit vector \(\hat{u}=u/\lVert u\rVert\). What is \(\lVert\hat{u}\rVert\)?

W2. Distance and nearest neighbor (Quiz 3 / Boyd 3.10–3.11 style). Arcata morning temperatures (°F) for three days: \[
a=(52,51,53),\qquad b=(54,50,55),\qquad c=(60,58,59).
\] A new day is \(x=(53,52,54)\).

Compute \(\lVert x-a\rVert\), \(\lVert x-b\rVert\), and \(\lVert x-c\rVert\) by hand or with software.
Which day is the nearest neighbor of \(x\)?
In one sentence, what does “nearest” mean here?

W3. Boolean distance (Boyd 3.1). Suppose \(x\) and \(y\) are Boolean \(n\)-vectors (entries only \(0\) or \(1\)).

Show that \(\lVert x-y\rVert^2\) equals the number of positions where \(x\) and \(y\) disagree.
Therefore \(\lVert x-y\rVert=\sqrt{k}\) where \(k\) is that disagreement count. For \(x=(1,0,1,1,0)\) and \(y=(1,1,0,1,0)\), find \(k\) and \(\lVert x-y\rVert\).

W4. RMS, average, and standard deviation (Boyd 3.15 setup). Let \[
x=(2,4,4,6).
\] (a) Compute \(\mathrm{avg}(x)\), \(\lVert x\rVert\), \(\mathrm{rms}(x)\), the de-meaned vector \(\tilde{x}\), and \(\mathrm{std}(x)\).

Check Boyd’s identity \(\mathrm{rms}(x)^2=\mathrm{avg}(x)^2+\mathrm{std}(x)^2\).
Interpret \(\mathrm{std}(x)\) in one short sentence for this data.

W5. Feature scale changes nearest neighbor (Quiz 3 C1.2 style). Two features: area (in \(1000\) ft²) and bedrooms. Houses: \[
h_1=(1.6,\ 2),\qquad h_2=(1.5,\ 2),\qquad h_3=(1.6,\ 4).
\] (a) Compute \(\lVert h_1-h_2\rVert\) and \(\lVert h_1-h_3\rVert\). Which house is nearer to \(h_1\)?

Now measure area in square feet instead, so the vectors become \[
\tilde{h}_1=(1600,\ 2),\qquad \tilde{h}_2=(1500,\ 2),\qquad \tilde{h}_3=(1600,\ 4).
\] Compute \(\lVert\tilde{h}_1-\tilde{h}_2\rVert\) and \(\lVert\tilde{h}_1-\tilde{h}_3\rVert\). Which house is nearer to \(\tilde{h}_1\) now?
What changed, and why does Boyd warn about units on heterogeneous features?

title: Lecture 07 — Norm, distance, RMS, and variation
text:
Check yourself
C1. Let \(w=(1,-2,2)\). Compute \(\lVert w\rVert\) by hand. Then write one Octave line and one Python line that compute it.
C2. Quiz 3 C1.1 style. Observation \(x=(1,2)\). Candidates: \[
z_1=(0,2),\quad z_2=(3,2),\quad z_3=(1,5),\quad z_4=(2,1),\quad z_5=(1,2.5).
\] Compute the five distances \(\lVert x-z_i\rVert\) (hand or software). Which candidate is nearest?
C3. Boyd 3.2 style. Let \(a\) be an \(n\)-vector and \(b\) an \(m\)-vector, and set \(x=(a,b)\) (stack). Express \(\mathrm{rms}(x)\) in terms of \(\mathrm{rms}(a)\), \(\mathrm{rms}(b)\), \(n\), and \(m\).
C4. For \(t=(10,10,10,14)\), find \(\mathrm{avg}(t)\) and \(\mathrm{std}(t)\). Use Boyd’s definition (RMS of the de-meaned vector).
C5. True or false, with one sentence: if \(\lVert x\rVert=\lVert y\rVert\), then \(x=y\) or \(x=-y\).






NoteAnswers (Check yourself only)





C1. \(\lVert w\rVert=\sqrt{1+4+4}=3\). Octave: norm([1;-2;2]). Python: np.linalg.norm(np.array([1.,-2.,2.])).
C2. Distances: \(1\), \(2\), \(3\), \(\sqrt{2}\approx 1.414\), \(0.5\). Nearest is \(z_5=(1,2.5)\).
C3. \(\mathrm{rms}(x)=\sqrt{\dfrac{n\,\mathrm{rms}(a)^2+m\,\mathrm{rms}(b)^2}{n+m}}\).
C4. \(\mathrm{avg}(t)=11\). De-meaned \((-1,-1,-1,3)\); \(\mathrm{std}(t)=\sqrt{(1+1+1+9)/4}=\sqrt{3}\).
C5. False. Example: \(x=(1,0)\) and \(y=(0,1)\) have the same norm but are neither equal nor negatives.

title: Course Syllabus
text:
Course Description (Catalog Description)
Euclidean spaces, matrices and matrix arithmetic, solving systems of equations, and eigenvalues and eigenvectors. Emphasis on applications and use of computation.
Division: Lower Division.
Weekly: Lecture 3 hrs.
Instruction Mode: Face to face only.
Prerequisite: (MATH 101 and MATH 101T) or MATH 102 or ALEKS PPL assessment score 78–100 or appropriate high school coursework. All prerequisite courses must be passed with a grade of C− or higher. See Math Placement and ALEKS PPL for details.
Note: if you plan to use MATH 107 as a prerequisite for another MATH, DATA, or STAT course, you must have a grade of C− or better in this course.

Course Learning Outcomes
By the end of this course, students will be able to:

Interpret matrices, vectors, and complex numbers, both algebraically and geometrically.
Solve systems of linear equations using row-reduction techniques by hand and with software.
Find eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a matrix by hand for a \(2\times 2\) matrix and with software for general cases.
Understand and apply eigenvalues and eigenvectors to solve problems.
Recognize special types of matrices and their properties, such as triangular, symmetric, and positive definite matrices.
Communicate in the language of linear algebra, including linear combination, subspace, span, independence, basis, and dimension.
Write or adapt programs to implement linear algebra concepts, such as matrix arithmetic, vectors, and plotting.
Apply linear algebra to real-world problems.
Learn independently as well as collaboratively. Develop study techniques that include pre- and post-reading of class materials and be able to critically analyze and implement solutions in a team setting.

Daily learning objectives for each meeting are on Lectures.


General Education & Institutional Learning Outcomes
This course fulfills Lower Division General Education Area 2 (Mathematics) and supports Cal Poly Humboldt’s Institutional Learning Outcomes related to quantitative reasoning, critical thinking, and communication.

title: Course Syllabus
text:
Course Materials & Workload
MATH 107 includes three weekly lecture meetings. Some Fridays (and a few other days) include a lab, quiz, or exam as marked on the schedule.
In this 3-unit course, students should expect to spend approximately 9 hours per week on course-related work, including time in class (3 hours) and time outside of class on reading, practice, labs, and exam preparation (6 hours).

Required Materials
Course website: Canvas and https://roverhol.github.io/math107
Textbooks (free):

Stephen Boyd and Lieven Vandenberghe, Introduction to Applied Linear Algebra: Vectors, Matrices, and Least Squares (VMLS).
Gilbert Strang, Introduction to Linear Algebra: selected free MIT samples only (§3.5, §6.1, and SVD slides), so you do not need to buy it.

Software: Octave, free to download at https://octave.org/. I will also provide an optional Python/Colab version of each lab.
Other Technology: A scientific calculator for in-class assessments and regular access to a computer with reliable internet. Bring a laptop on lab days, or let me know a day ahead that I should bring one for you to use. Please bring paper and a pen or pencil to class each day.


Access & Affordability
Students who do not have personal access to required technology may use computers either in campus labs or checked out from the library. Calculators are also available for check out from the library’s front desk. If you want to get a free used computer, please check to see if our campus’s Reusable Office Supply Exchange (ROSE) has one available.


Fees
There are no additional course fees beyond standard tuition and registration fees.

Grade Mode: Letter grade by default. Students may elect Credit/No Credit grading according to university deadlines and procedures.
A minimum grade of C− is required for the course to count as a prerequisite for other MATH or DATA classes.
If you stop attending class and stop doing assignments without communicating with me, you will receive a grade of WU (Withdrawal Unsatisfactory). Please communicate with me early if you are having difficulties: it’s possible that I can help you get back on track, or help you obtain a more appropriate grade (W or I) for your situation.



Attendance & Participation
Regular attendance and active participation are required because they are essential for the success of everyone in this course. Up to 10 days may be missed without penalty to your course grade: these days should be reserved for use in times of illness or other obligations.
If you must miss class, you are responsible for obtaining notes from me or a classmate and keeping up with course material.

title: Course Syllabus
text:
Late or Missed Work Policies
The policies for late or missed work are as follows:

Lecture attendance is required, but I know that sometimes you will need to miss class due to illness or other emergencies. Each student may miss up to 10 lecture days without penalty and without contacting me. Reserve these days for emergencies. In my experience, it is rare for a student to succeed if they regularly miss class or are absent for more than two weeks, so if you find yourself in that situation, please communicate with me and your advisor so we can help you find a solution.
Quizzes are in the first 10 minutes of class. The lowest two quiz scores are dropped. If you must miss a quiz due to illness or another emergency, please contact me to arrange a makeup.
Labs are due on the dates on the schedule. After a week, late labs are not accepted.
Capstone work is due on the dates on the schedule. Late project work cannot be turned in due to the end of the semester and course grades being due. If you are unable to complete the project in time, you should consider whether your situation is such that an Incomplete grade is appropriate. This would give you more time to complete the course.
Midterms and the final exam are required. If you need to miss a midterm due to illness or another emergency, communicate with me as soon as possible to reschedule.

Note: Technology issues (internet access, device failure, software problems) are not automatically considered valid excuses for late or missed work; students are expected to plan accordingly.


AI Policy
Much of your course grade will be based on work you produce in class (quizzes and exams) without having the option of using AI as a resource.
Outside of in-class assessments, you may use AI, such as NotebookLM or ChatGPT, to help you learn the material or to get unstuck on labs or the capstone.
For work that you do at home that is turned in for a grade I have two requirements:

If you used AI, acknowledge this briefly in the document (you don’t need to state in detail how you used AI or give your prompts, just the name of the AI service you used).
Be responsible for the correctness and appropriateness of all (AI-assisted or not) materials you turn in.

I may use AI to assist me in my delivery of the course material, such as asking whether an assignment is appropriate for a college-level course or whether the wording of a quiz question could be improved. I will not use AI to grade your work or use an AI detection tool to check your work.

Reading: Boyd 1.2–1.3
By the end of class, students should be able to:

Add, subtract, and scale vectors.
Interpret those operations geometrically.
Plot vectors in \(\mathbb{R}^2\) and recognize corresponding operations in \(\mathbb{R}^3\).
Check whether an answer has sensible dimensions and units.

title: Lectures
text: Week 2

title: Lectures
text:
Mon Aug 31 — Linear combinations
Lecture 03 page
Reading: Linear combinations (class notes), Lab 0, and Lachniet Ch. 1 (Getting Started).
Note: No prior coding assumed. Lachniet is one PDF on Resources; chapters are listed here.
By the end of class, students should be able to:

Form and interpret linear combinations.
Explain the meaning of coefficients in context.
Enter, index, and modify vectors in Octave or Python.
Perform vector arithmetic and create a basic plot.
Modify supplied code and explain its output or error message.

title: Lectures
text:
Wed Sep 2 — Inner product
Lecture 04 page
Reading: Boyd 1.4; Boyd 1.1 stack and slice (Quiz 1 prep)
By the end of class, students should be able to:

Compute a dot product.
Interpret it as a weighted sum.
Interpret its sign and magnitude as alignment.
Recognize orthogonal vectors from a zero dot product.

title: Lectures
section: Fri Sep 4 — Linear and affine functions
text:
Fri Sep 4 — Linear and affine functions
Lecture 05 page
Reading: Boyd 2.1 and 2.3
Note: Boyd’s calculus-dependent Taylor-approximation material is optional.
By the end of class, students should be able to:

Distinguish linear from affine functions in examples.
Test superposition numerically on simple functions.
Construct a function \(a^{\mathsf{T}}x+b\) for a contextual quantity.
Evaluate a model by hand and computationally.

title: Lectures
text: Week 3

title: Lectures
section: Mon Sep 7 — Labor Day — no class
text: Mon Sep 7 — Labor Day — no class

title: Lectures
section: Wed Sep 9 — Linear functions in applications
text:
Wed Sep 9 — Linear functions in applications
Lecture 06 page
Reading: Applications of linear and affine models
By the end of class, students should be able to:

Model a score, cost, prediction, or aggregate quantity.
Interpret model coefficients and intercepts.
Compare outputs from competing models.
State a reasonable limitation or assumption of a linear model.

title: Lectures
section: Fri Sep 11 — Norm, distance, RMS, and variation
text:
Fri Sep 11 — Norm, distance, RMS, and variation
Lecture 07 page
Reading: Boyd 3.1–3.3
By the end of class, students should be able to:

Compute vector norms and distances.
Interpret norm and distance geometrically and contextually.
Relate norm to RMS and, where appropriate, variation around an average.
Use software to calculate distances in dimensions too large for hand computation.

title: Lectures
text: Week 4

title: Lectures
text:
Mon Sep 14 — Angle and similarity
Lecture 08 page
Reading: Boyd 3.4
By the end of class, students should be able to:

Compute cosine similarity or an angle between vectors.
Distinguish closeness in position from similarity in direction.
Choose an appropriate similarity measure for a stated purpose.
Explain why normalization may change a comparison.

title: Lectures
text:
Wed Sep 16 — Nearest neighbors
Lecture 09 page
Reading: Boyd 4.1
Note: Possible contexts: species measurements, geographic sites, songs, or sensor readings.
By the end of class, students should be able to:

Formulate a nearest-neighbor question using vectors.
Find a nearest neighbor in a small dataset by hand.
Explain how feature scale can affect the answer.
Justify a choice of distance or similarity measure.

title: Lectures
text:
Fri Sep 18 — Clustering and \(k\)-means
Lecture 10 page
Reading: Boyd 4.2–4.3
Note: Use a small dataset students can visualize.
By the end of class, students should be able to:

Explain the goal of clustering.
Compute one assignment/update iteration of \(k\)-means.
Interpret a centroid as a vector.
Recognize that clustering output depends on representation, scaling, and initialization.

title: Lectures
text: Week 5

title: Lectures
text:
Mon Sep 21 — Finding similar things
Lecture 11 page
Reading: Lab 1 and Lachniet Ch. 1 (vectors, matrix storage, indexing, plots).
By the end of class, students should be able to:

Load and inspect a dataset represented by vectors.
Compute many distances with Octave or Python.
Adapt supplied code to identify nearest observations or clusters.
Validate computational output on a small hand-checkable subset.
Interpret results in the original context.

title: Lectures
section: Wed Sep 23 — Linear dependence as redundancy
text:
Wed Sep 23 — Linear dependence as redundancy
Lecture 12 page
Reading: Boyd 5.1
By the end of class, students should be able to:

Recognize simple dependent and independent collections.
Construct a dependence relationship.
Interpret dependence as redundant information.
Explain why redundancy matters in data, measurement, and computation.

title: Lectures
section: Fri Sep 25 — Span, independence, and subspaces
text:
Fri Sep 25 — Span, independence, and subspaces
Lecture 13 page
Reading: Traditional vocabulary supplement to Boyd
By the end of class, students should be able to:

Define span using linear combinations.
Determine whether a vector lies in a simple span.
Interpret spans geometrically as lines, planes, or higher-dimensional collections.
Recognize basic subspaces and distinguish them from shifted lines or planes.

title: Lectures
text: Week 6

title: Lectures
section: Mon Sep 28 — Basis, dimension, and orthonormal vectors
text:
Mon Sep 28 — Basis, dimension, and orthonormal vectors
Lecture 14 page
Reading: Boyd 5.2–5.3
Note: Gram–Schmidt is a important application.
By the end of class, students should be able to:

Explain what a basis accomplishes.
Identify a basis and dimension in simple examples.
Use linear combination, span, subspace, independence, basis, and dimension accurately.
Recognize an orthonormal collection.
Explain why orthonormal coordinates are convenient for measurement and reconstruction.

title: Lectures
text:
Wed Sep 30 — Unit I synthesis
Lecture 15 page
Reading: Unit I synthesis (no new Boyd section)
By the end of class, students should be able to:

Connect distance, similarity, span, and independence.
Select an appropriate vector tool for a new problem.
Move between algebraic, geometric, computational, and contextual representations.
Diagnose and explain common errors.

title: Lectures
text:
Fri Oct 2 — Midterm 1 review
Lecture 16 page
Reading: Unit I review
Note: Full review day.
By the end of class, students should be able to:

Retrieve major Unit I concepts without notes.
Solve mixed rather than chapter-isolated problems.
Explain reasoning collaboratively.
Identify gaps and make a targeted study plan.

title: Lectures
text: Week 7

title: Lectures
text:
Mon Oct 5 — Midterm 1
Lecture 17 page
Reading: Midterm 1 (in class)
By the end of class, students should be able to:

Compute with vectors and linear functions.
Interpret vector operations in context.
Analyze distance, similarity, span, and independence.
Select and communicate an appropriate method.

title: Lectures
section: Wed Oct 7 — Matrices as data and structured objects
text:
Wed Oct 7 — Matrices as data and structured objects
Lecture 18 page
Reading: Boyd 6.1–6.3
By the end of class, students should be able to:

Identify matrix dimensions, rows, columns, and entries.
Represent datasets, networks, images, or systems as matrices.
Perform matrix addition, scaling, and transposition.
Recognize zero, identity, diagonal, triangular, symmetric, and sparse matrices.
Explain one practical consequence of matrix structure.

title: Lectures
text:
Fri Oct 9 — Matrix-vector multiplication
Lecture 19 page
Reading: Boyd 6.4
Note: Connect directly back to Week 1 linear combinations.
By the end of class, students should be able to:

Compute \(Ax\) by hand for a small matrix.
Interpret \(Ax\) as a linear combination of the columns of \(A\).
Interpret \(A\) as an input-output transformation.
Explain how the dimensions of \(A\) determine the input and output spaces.

title: Lectures
text: Week 8

title: Lectures
text:
Mon Oct 12 — Transforming space
Lecture 20 page
Reading: Boyd 7.1–7.2, Lab 2, and Lachniet Ch. 2 (matrices and linear-algebra computations).
Note: Include a 3D or coordinate-system example.
By the end of class, students should be able to:

Predict the effect of scaling, reflection, shear, and rotation matrices.
Apply matrices to many 2D or 3D points at once.
Plot and compare original and transformed objects.
Adapt a short program that implements a transformation.
Interpret a matrix as a coordinate or physical-space transformation.

title: Lectures
text:
Wed Oct 14 — Systems and \(Ax=b\)
Lecture 21 page
Reading: Boyd 8.3
By the end of class, students should be able to:

Translate equations or contextual constraints into \(Ax=b\).
Interpret \(Ax=b\) as asking whether \(b\) belongs to the span of the columns of \(A\).
Classify systems as square, underdetermined, or overdetermined.
Anticipate circumstances producing zero, one, or many solutions.

title: Lectures
text:
Fri Oct 16 — Gaussian elimination
Lecture 22 page
Reading: Gaussian elimination (class notes) and Lachniet Ch. 2 (solving systems, RREF).
Note: Hand work first; software later.
By the end of class, students should be able to:

Perform elementary row operations.
Reduce a small augmented matrix to echelon form.
Solve a small system using back substitution.
Explain why row operations preserve the solution set.

title: Lectures
text: Week 9

title: Lectures
section: Mon Oct 19 — RREF, pivots, free variables, and software
text:
Mon Oct 19 — RREF, pivots, free variables, and software
Lecture 23 page
Reading: RREF and software solvers; Lachniet Ch. 2 (linear-system commands).
Note: For Python, provide an RREF helper or use SymPy rather than making novices implement RREF.
By the end of class, students should be able to:

Interpret reduced row echelon form.
Identify pivot and free variables.
Describe a solution set parametrically.
Distinguish inconsistent, unique, and infinite-solution cases.
Use software to solve or row-reduce a system and verify the answer using a residual.

title: Lectures
text:
Wed Oct 21 — Linear dynamical systems
Lecture 24 page
Reading: Boyd 9.1–9.3
By the end of class, students should be able to:

Represent an evolving system as \(x_{t+1}=Ax_t\).
Interpret the state vector and transition matrix.
Build a transition matrix from a flow description.
Compute and interpret the next few states.

title: Lectures
section: Fri Oct 23 — Simulation and long-run behavior
text:
Fri Oct 23 — Simulation and long-run behavior
Lecture 25 page
Reading: Simulation of linear dynamics
Note: Do not explain the eigenvalue mechanism yet; let students form conjectures.
By the end of class, students should be able to:

Simulate many time steps computationally.
Plot state components through time.
Recognize stabilization, growth, decay, or oscillation.
Conduct a simple what-if simulation.
State limitations of a linear dynamical model.

title: Lectures
text: Week 10

title: Lectures
section: Mon Oct 26 — Predict a system through time
text:
Mon Oct 26 — Predict a system through time
Lecture 26 page
Reading: Lab 3, Lachniet Ch. 2 (matrix operations), and Lachniet’s introductory programming/loops material.
Note: This creates the eigenvalue “mystery.”
By the end of class, students should be able to:

Implement a linear dynamical model.
Write or complete a short iterative calculation.
Validate the first steps by hand.
Compare results under altered parameters or initial states.
Record an unexplained long-run pattern for later investigation.

title: Lectures
text:
Wed Oct 28 — Matrix multiplication
Lecture 27 page
Reading: Boyd 10.1
By the end of class, students should be able to:

Determine whether a product is defined and give its dimensions.
Compute a small matrix product.
Interpret \(ABx\) as a sequence of transformations.
Explain why matrix multiplication is generally not commutative.

title: Lectures
section: Fri Oct 30 — Composition and matrix powers
text:
Fri Oct 30 — Composition and matrix powers
Lecture 28 page
Reading: Boyd 10.2–10.3
Note: Return to the dynamics lab from a new viewpoint.
By the end of class, students should be able to:

Combine multistage processes using a matrix product.
Connect \(A^k x\) to repeated dynamics.
Interpret selected entries of a matrix product or power.
Recognize how network and transition information accumulates through powers.

title: Lectures
text: Week 11

title: Lectures
section: Mon Nov 2 — Same mathematics, very different computational cost
text:
Mon Nov 2 — Same mathematics, very different computational cost
Lecture 29 page
Reading: Boyd’s \(ab^{\mathsf{T}}c\) example (micro-lab)
Note: Precursor to the capstone.
By the end of class, students should be able to:

Compare algebraically equivalent orders of computation.
Count intermediate values that must be stored.
Measure runtime for increasing problem sizes.
Explain why forming a large intermediate matrix may be wasteful.
Choose a computational order and justify it quantitatively.

title: Lectures
text:
Wed Nov 4 — Inverses and solving
Lecture 30 page
Reading: Boyd 11.1–11.3
By the end of class, students should be able to:

Interpret an inverse as undoing a transformation.
Determine whether a simple matrix is invertible.
Connect invertibility to uniqueness of \(Ax=b\).
Explain why solving \(Ax=b\) is generally preferable computationally to explicitly calculating \(A^{-1}\).

title: Lectures
section: Fri Nov 6 — Rank, column space, null space, and basis connections
text:
Fri Nov 6 — Rank, column space, null space, and basis connections
Lecture 31 page
Reading: Boyd plus selected portions of Strang §3.5, especially rank, column space, null space, basis, and dimension.
Note: Not a full four-subspaces theory unit. Row space and left nullspace are enrichment, not quiz material.
By the end of class, students should be able to:

Interpret column space and null space through \(Ax=b\) and \(Ax=0\).
Determine rank from pivots or independent columns.
Find simple bases for column or null spaces.
Connect rank to consistency, independence, and dimension.
Use subspace, basis, dimension, rank, column space, and null space correctly.

title: Lectures
text: Week 12

title: Lectures
section: Mon Nov 9 — Determinants, geometry, and invertibility
text:
Mon Nov 9 — Determinants, geometry, and invertibility
Lecture 32 page
Reading: Determinants (class notes)
By the end of class, students should be able to:

Compute determinants of \(2\times 2\) and simple triangular matrices.
Interpret determinant magnitude as area or volume scaling.
Connect determinant zero with lost dimension and noninvertibility.
Recognize the determinant of a triangular matrix from its diagonal.
Connect determinants to the coming characteristic equation.

title: Lectures
section: Wed Nov 11 — Veterans Day — no class
text: Wed Nov 11 — Veterans Day — no class

title: Lectures
section: Fri Nov 13 — Midterm 2 review and synthesis
text:
Fri Nov 13 — Midterm 2 review and synthesis
Lecture 33 page
Reading: Unit II review
Note: Full review day.
By the end of class, students should be able to:

Connect transformations, systems, dynamics, rank, inverses, and determinants.
Compare hand and computational solution methods.
Interpret software output instead of merely reporting it.
Solve a new application requiring more than one concept.

title: Lectures
text: Week 13

title: Lectures
text:
Mon Nov 16 — Midterm 2
Lecture 34 page
Reading: Midterm 2 (in class)
By the end of class, students should be able to:

Analyze matrices as transformations and models.
Solve and interpret systems.
Use matrix products, powers, rank, inverses, and determinants appropriately.
Interpret computational results in context.

title: Lectures
section: Wed Nov 18 — Eigenvectors as persistent directions
text:
Wed Nov 18 — Eigenvectors as persistent directions
Lecture 35 page
Reading: Beginning of Strang §6.1 — \(Ax=\lambda x\), eigenvectors, and dynamics.
Note: Start with the unexplained behavior from Lab 3. The free PDF is only §6.1.
By the end of class, students should be able to:

Explain geometrically what makes \(v\) an eigenvector.
Verify a proposed eigenpair.
Find \(\lambda\) when an eigenvector is given.
Connect eigenvectors to repeated transformations and steady directions.
Recognize that a rotation may have no real eigenvector, motivating complex numbers.

title: Lectures
section: Fri Nov 20 — Characteristic equation, \(2\times 2\) eigenproblems, and complex numbers
text:
Fri Nov 20 — Characteristic equation, \(2\times 2\) eigenproblems, and complex numbers
Lecture 36 page
Reading: Strang §6.1, characteristic equation and the complex-eigenvalue (\(90^\circ\) rotation) example.
Note: Meets the explicit hand-calculation and complex-number CLOs. The same free §6.1 file is used Nov 16–20.
By the end of class, students should be able to:

Interpret \(a+bi\) algebraically and as a point/vector in the complex plane.
Perform the basic complex arithmetic needed for eigenvalue calculations.
Form and solve \(\det(A-\lambda I)=0\) for a \(2\times 2\) matrix.
Find corresponding eigenvectors.
Check real or complex eigenpairs by substitution.

title: Lectures
text: Week 15

title: Lectures
section: Mon Nov 30 — Why did the system behave that way?
text:
Mon Nov 30 — Why did the system behave that way?
Lecture 37 page
Reading: Strang §6.1, Lab 4, and Lachniet Ch. 5 (eigenvalues/eigenvectors).
Note: Normal modes are an application/demo, not a differential-equations derivation. Students then use software in Lab 4.
By the end of class, students should be able to:

Compute eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a general matrix with software.
Verify \(Av\approx\lambda v\) numerically.
Use dominant eigenbehavior to explain a simulated system.
Interpret complex eigenvalues as rotation/oscillation behavior.
Explore a symmetric-matrix or normal-mode example and observe orthogonal eigenvectors.

title: Lectures
section: Wed Dec 2 — When \(Ax=b\) has no exact solution
text:
Wed Dec 2 — When \(Ax=b\) has no exact solution
Lecture 38 page
Reading: Boyd 12.1
By the end of class, students should be able to:

Recognize an inconsistent overdetermined system.
Formulate the least-squares objective \(\min_x \lVert Ax-b\rVert\).
Interpret the fitted vector as the closest attainable vector.
Interpret the residual geometrically.
Distinguish an exact solution from a best approximate solution.

title: Lectures
section: Fri Dec 4 — Least squares, data fitting, and positive definiteness
text:
Fri Dec 4 — Least squares, data fitting, and positive definiteness
Lecture 39 page
Reading: Boyd 12.2–12.4 and 13.1, class notes on symmetric and positive-definite matrices, Lab 5, and Lachniet Ch. 2 (least-squares / data-fitting exercises).
Note: Use a small real dataset. Positive definiteness is from Boyd and class notes, not later Strang sections.
By the end of class, students should be able to:

Compute a least-squares solution with Octave or Python.
Plot observed and fitted values.
Interpret residuals and an RMS error in context.
Check the residual’s orthogonality to the columns of \(A\).
Evaluate whether a fitted model is useful rather than merely reporting coefficients.
Recognize that \(A^{\mathsf{T}}A\) is symmetric positive semidefinite, explain \(x^{\mathsf{T}}A^{\mathsf{T}}Ax=\lVert Ax\rVert^2\), and recognize that \(A^{\mathsf{T}}A\) is positive definite when \(A\) has linearly independent columns.

title: Lectures
text: Week 16

title: Lectures
section: Mon Dec 7 — SVD, low-rank approximation, and capstone launch
text:
Mon Dec 7 — SVD, low-rank approximation, and capstone launch
Lecture 40 page
Reading: Selected slides from the Strang/MIT SVD slides (not all 17 pages), capstone launch, Lachniet Ch. 5 (SVD) and Ch. 7 (image compression).
By the end of class, students should be able to:

Interpret \(A=U\Sigma V^{\mathsf{T}}\) conceptually.
Construct a rank-\(k\) approximation computationally.
Compare singular-value decay for an image/frame and a frame-difference matrix.
Encode three frames either independently or as \(F_1\), \(D_2\), \(D_3\).
Compare reconstruction error and storage for the two approaches.
Formulate a capstone question involving accuracy, storage, runtime, and resource use.

title: Lectures
text:
Wed Dec 9 — Capstone studio
Lecture 41 page
Reading: Capstone (no new mathematics)
By the end of class, students should be able to:

Implement and validate a low-rank computational strategy.
Measure approximation error, storage, and runtime.
Separate one-time factorization cost from repeated-use cost.
Compare theoretical operation/storage counts with empirical measurements.
Debug and refine an analysis collaboratively while retaining individual understanding.

title: Lectures
section: Fri Dec 11 — Capstone presentations / gallery walk
text:
Fri Dec 11 — Capstone presentations / gallery walk
Lecture 42 page
Reading: Capstone presentations
Note: Pair lightning talks or gallery walk.
By the end of class, students should be able to:

Explain the problem and why SVD or another linear-algebra tool was appropriate.
Present quantitative evidence about accuracy and cost.
Defend a choice of rank or representation.
Evaluate classmates’ methods constructively.
Communicate the practical value and limitations of the result.

title: Lectures
text:
Fri Dec 11 — Cumulative final review
Lecture 43 page
Reading: Cumulative review
Note: No routine quiz or new content.
By the end of class, students should be able to:

Connect vectors, systems, transformations, dynamics, eigenvectors, least squares, and SVD.
Select an appropriate method for a new situation.
Decide what should be done by hand and what should be delegated to software.
Interpret mathematical and computational results.
Create a targeted final-exam study plan.

title: Resources
text:
Python / Google Colab
If you choose Python, use Google Colab for all Python labs. Colab is a hosted Jupyter notebook; you do not need to install Python locally. Each lab will have a Colab version alongside the Octave version.



Role
Tool
Link




Where we write and run Python
Google Colab
colab.google


Organize and prepare tabular data
Polars
Getting started


Vectors, matrices, and linear algebra
NumPy
Beginner guide; later, linear algebra


Visualize and communicate results
Plotnine
Introductory guide



Polars is for real tables: reading files, selecting columns, filtering, transforming, and handing numerical columns to NumPy. NumPy is for arrays, indexing, and later solve, eig, lstsq, svd, norms, and determinants. Plotnine is for scatterplots, line plots, fitted relationships, residual plots, clustering graphics, and other standard figures; it uses a grammar-of-graphics syntax and works directly with Polars DataFrames.
As with Lachniet, these pages support syntax. The lab handouts are the assigned work.
